articles.title_orig: The Fed's AI Bank Run Nightmare Is Suddenly Coming True
articles.title_zh: The Fed's AI Bank Run Nightmare Is Suddenly Coming True
articles.content_orig:
Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller on Wednesday called for aggressive action against inflation , saying the central bank need to "shock people" as prices continue to rise more than he expected.
In the near term, the policymaker told CNBC in a live interview that a half-percentage-point increase in the Fed's benchmark rate is probably necessary at the Dec. 8-9 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee.
He said the Fed needs to reverse the three quarter-point reductions from last year and may need to do more.
"I'm very, very concerned about inflation. It's kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it's spreading out," Waller told CNBC's Steve Liesman during a "Squawk Box" interview. "If you really want to get it down, you've got to start taking more aggressive actions."
"You might need to, like, shock people," he said.
Futures prices are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point hike at the FOMC's Dec. 8-9 meeting. They also are anticipating another move in January, followed by at least one additional increase before the end of 2027, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge.
Waller said the Fed wouldn't necessarily have to approve a half-point hike in December if it raised rates by a quarter point and signaled another move coming in January. However, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has been against that kind of forward guidance on grounds that it ties policymakers' hands.
"If you're not going to signal this very clearly to markets, you're going in January, my view is then you have to go 50 [basis points] in December to put it in place and get it done," he said.
Recent statements from other central bankers indicate a range of opinions , though most agree that more policy tightening is needed to bring down inflation.
In a speech Tuesday, St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem suggested as many as four hikes by the spring of 2027. Some Fed officials, including regional presidents Beth Hammack of Cleveland and Lorie Logan of Dallas, have endorsed more gradual tightening.
However, continued inflation above the Fed's 2% target might push officials into a more aggressive stance.
The FOMC approved its first interest rate hike in more than three years in September, and then held rates steady at its October meeting. While inflation has continued to run hot since then, other Fed officials seem less eager to drop the policy hammer as heavily as Waller.
"I don't think the situation calls for dramatic action," New York Fed President John Williams said Tuesday in a conversation with Axios. "I think what we've been doing over the last past few months is ... working well. We're collecting the data, analyzing it, having the debate and making a decision."
The Fed in 2025 approved three rate cuts amid worries over the labor market and the belief that inflation would continue to moderate toward the central bank's 2% goal.
However, inflation reignited earlier this year after the strikes the U.S. and Israel launched against Iran in late February. Energy prices spiked while tariff impacts lingered, keeping most inflation readings above 3% .
"First of all, you've got to take back the three insurance cuts we put in last year," Waller said. "If the policy rate last summer in 2025 wasn't bringing inflation down, getting back to that isn't going to bring it down. So we may have to go above ... three hikes plus maybe some more to get it to start actually coming back down."
The FOMC later Wednesday will release minutes from the October meeting.

articles.title_orig: Trump personally greeted by President Xi upon arrival in China
articles.title_zh: Trump personally greeted by President Xi upon arrival in China
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday morning ahead of historic trilateral talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin.
Xi earlier welcomed President Donald Trump on the tarmac, which he said was a sign of reciprocity after Trump personally greeted him at the airport during a visit to the U.S. in September.
Trump is attending a welcome banquet alongside Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
Trump is in China for the APEC summit, which President Xi opened with calls for free trade and greater cooperation around artificial intelligence. Highly anticipated talks with Xi and Putin are set for Thursday.
Xi said Thursday's leaders' meeting would discuss "measures to expand mutual openness, explore paths for innovation-driven growth, and broaden practical cooperation in various fields," according to Chinese state media. The Chinese president told Trump he wanted to "advance a constructive, strategic and stable relationship between China and the US based on respect, fairness and reciprocity," according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua. Trump said he was confident the visit would advance bilateral relations and prove successful, Xinhua reported.
Xi said: "We should actively build partnerships for scientific and technological innovation, deepen cooperation in the digital economy and artificial intelligence and promote a green and low-carbon transition."
Putin has also addressed the summit , saying sanctions imposed on Russia have backfired and strengthened his nation.
The much-anticipated meeting between the three world leaders is set to take place on Thursday, with discussions expected to center on the Iran war and Russia's war in Ukraine.
Though expectations for any concrete outcome are low, Trump, Xi and Putin are expected to hold in-depth discussions on issues crucial for world peace and strategic stability, a spokesperson for China's foreign ministry said Monday.
North Korean leader Kim Jong-Un could attend the summit, which is a forum of 21 APEC member economies.
Trump flew in from Manila, Philippines, where he started a three-day visit to Asia and met key regional allies including Japan, India and Australia.
The APEC host city Shenzhen has been dubbed one of China's "Silicon Valleys" and has been a major hub for China's internet and artificial intelligence companies.
Beijing will position itself against what it calls "unilateralism and protectionism," with trade, artificial intelligence, and the Middle East expected to dominate the meeting's agenda.
Xi held several bilateral meetings with leaders on the sidelines Wednesday, including South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, with whom he discussed trade and commerce. Seoul's readout of the meeting also said the pair discussed peace on the Korean Peninsula, but this was omitted from Beijing's record of the talks.
The Chinese leader also met Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Vietnamese President To Lam earlier in the week.
Xi met with Putin earlier Wednesday, before Trump's arrival. The Chinese president called for greater cooperation between the two countries and spoke of providing a more stable and predictable business environment, according to Chinese state media, while promoting a "multipolar world and democratization of international relations."
Putin said Russia was looking to expand cooperation in trade, energy and education. The reports did not address Russia's war in Ukraine or the Iran war.
Trump will also hold bilateral talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping, amid hopes the pair can secure a lasting trade truce beyond January 2027. The meeting comes as the U.S. seeks to curb exports of artificial intelligence chips and amid concerns that Nvidia chips may have been diverted to China.

articles.title_orig: Apple restores services after internal update caused outages
articles.title_zh: Apple restores services after internal update caused outages
articles.content_orig:
Apple said it has restored all services after users reported issues with Apple Pay, Apple Support, iCloud and other products on Tuesday.
A spokesperson for the company told CBS News in an email that its services are "green across the board," referring to the System Status page on Apple's website, as of approximately 5:46 p.m. ET.
Thousands of people reported issues with Apple services on Tuesday, according to the tracking site Downdetector.com . The reports started to spike before noon ET and lasted several hours before tapering off in the afternoon, the site shows.
By 4:45 p.m. ET, Apple's system status page showed problems with iCloud sign-in and "AppleCare on device" had been resolved. However, some services, including Apple Business and Apple School Manager, were still experiencing issues, according to the tech giant.
The issues were not the result of a cyberattack, according to the spokesperson.
Apple is the latest company to experience service disruptions following a string of outages that affected everything from air travel to Microsoft email. On Monday, customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and other major financial institutions also reported service issues affecting bank deposits and Zelle transfers.
Users also reported issues accessing Gmail on Tuesday. In a statement shared on X, Google said it isn't "currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption" and encouraged users to check its workplace status dashboard for updates.

articles.title_orig: Trump is greeted by Xi Jinping and meets with Canada’s Mark Carney as the China leg of his Asia trip gets underway
articles.title_zh: Trump is greeted by Xi Jinping and meets with Canada’s Mark Carney as the China leg of his Asia trip gets underway
articles.content_orig:

Donald Trump , Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin have converged in the Chinese city of Shenzhen for a rare meeting that has drawn comparisons with the Yalta Conference, which helped shape the world after the Second World War.
But the three leaders may have far less power to reshape global politics than the spectacle of their meeting suggests.
Xi is set to host the Russian and US leaders at this year's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum , which Beijing has hailed as being of “groundbreaking significance” in promoting world peace and stability.
As the Ukraine war drags on and tensions between the US and Iran simmer, all eyes are on Thursday's unprecedented trilateral meeting, which has drawn comparisons, particularly in Russia, with the 1945 Yalta Conference between the so-called Big Three – the US, the UK and the then Soviet Union – to discuss the fate of postwar Europe.
But unlike the wartime allies at Yalta, analysts tell The Independent the summit may be more consequential for its symbolism than its agreements, with each leader seeking individual gains despite their own vulnerabilities.
For China , the meeting comes amid pressure at home from slowing growth, with retail spending and investment weakening amid a prolonged property slump.
Its economy is still growing at more than four per cent, largely driven by surging exports that are provoking a backlash from trading partners.
Hosting Trump and Putin offers Xi an opportunity to demonstrate to the Chinese public that Beijing is operating at the highest levels of global diplomacy.
It is particularly important in the run-up to next year's Party Congress, where Chinese Communist Party leaders will select the next slate of leaders and are likely to grant Xi an unprecedented fourth term.
On Wednesday, Xi urged Asia-Pacific economies to deepen cooperation to keep global supply chains stable, warning against rising unilateralism and protectionism.
“Global growth lacks momentum, and unilateralism and protectionism are rampant,” Xi said at the CEO Summit in Shenzhen, referring to the Trump administration's tariffs on China, along with growing US technology restrictions, which have disrupted global supply chains.
“For Putin, it plays into his claims of great power status while distracting from the quagmire of his Ukrainian misadventure. For the host, Xi, it provides the appearance of China shaping the world order as an equal to the United States ,” Oskanian says.
For Trump, he adds, the meeting would provide a stage on which to perform his role as a "dealmaker" following what he describes as a "humiliating defeat in the mid-terms".
This marks Trump's first trip to Asia since his Republican Party's defeat in the midterm elections and after allegations that Nvidia founder Jensen Huang was dating a suspected Chinese spy – news that sent shockwaves through American political, diplomatic, and trade circles.
“The trilateral meeting between Trump-Xi-Putin will overwhelm the narrative of the Apec summit. This meeting appeals to all three leaders, each for their own reasons,” Ryan Hass, a China expert at the Brookings Institution, says .
“Trump will be eager to turn the page from his recent midterm election setback and reassert himself as a central figure on the world stage,” he adds.
It could be a case of the Chinese aphorism “all thunder, no rain”.
The previous two summits, in Beijing and Washington , ended without substantive breakthroughs, as the sides appeared content to prioritise optics over substance.
“Theoretically, there is much for the two leaders to discuss – everything from the risks of AI to global hotspots – but it seems more likely than not that these two leaders will miss the moment, again,” says American political scientist and sinologist Jonathan A Czin, calling it “pantomime diplomacy”.
Swaran Singh, a professor at the Jawaharlal Nehru University in Delhi, says Trump would approach the trilateral meeting with the aim of finding resolutions to the wars in Ukraine and Iran , adding that the talks were taking place at the US president's initiative.
“If you look at what can happen in this meeting, one can easily learn from what happened in their bilateral meeting last year in August in Alaska . Nothing came out of it,” he says .
“We cannot ever expect that Apec will deliver any breakthroughs. It will always be very piecemeal, behind-the-curtain, slow-motion activities that will happen.
“Therefore, they will definitely have a declaration, and it'll be more sentimental in terms of semantics expressing intent rather than actionable things," Singh adds.
One area where the limits of Trump's dealmaking ambitions could become particularly apparent is nuclear arms control, with Beijing showing little appetite for restrictions on its rapidly expanding arsenal.
The Chinese foreign ministry has, however, pushed back against suggestions of trilateral nuclear talks , citing the disparity between its arsenal and those of the US and Russia.
China has around 600 nuclear warheads , compared with 3,700 for the US and 4,400 for Russia. Despite an 80 per cent reduction in the US stockpile since the fall of the Berlin Wall, Beijing continues to demand further cuts before joining arms control talks, even as its own arsenal has roughly tripled since 2020.
“Beijing is unlikely to slow its nuclear expansion soon,” Tong Zhao, a nuclear policy expert at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, says , pointing to Beijing's continued investment in infrastructure for producing fissile material and researching, testing and manufacturing nuclear warheads.
China's latest Five-Year Plan, covering 2026 to 2030, explicitly commits to "strengthen and enlarge" its strategic deterrence.
“Beijing has resisted trilateral talks in particular. It insists that Washington and Moscow bear primary responsibility for arms control and rejects any format implying that China owes comparable obligations. Substantive outcomes at a trilateral summit, such as arsenal limits or greater transparency, are therefore highly unlikely,” Zhao adds.
Trump also wants to start nuclear talks with Russia following the expiration of the START treaty on 5 February this year. The two countries currently have no nuclear arms control agreement.
It marked the first time since 1972 that there have been no legally binding limits constraining the nuclear arsenals of the world's two largest nuclear powers.
Prof Singh says: “Trump is restarting arms control negotiations with Russia not simply to put certain control on Russian nuclear weapons, but also to bring China into nuclear negotiations and build consensus to deny Iran any possibility of building nuclear weapons."
However, Zhao says the three leaders could agree on smaller measures to reduce nuclear risks, including keeping artificial intelligence out of decisions to launch nuclear weapons and establishing advance notification of missile launches.
A trilateral missile notification agreement would be particularly significant, building on existing arrangements between the US and Russia, and Russia and China, while closing a gap between Washington and Beijing.
The leaders could also reaffirm the Cold War-era Ronald Reagan-Mikhail Gorbachev declaration that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought”, although Zhao cautioned that such pledges have limited value without concrete action.
More meaningful progress, Zhao argues, would involve agreeing on what constitutes a nuclear threat and how to prevent nuclear signalling from being used as a tool of coercion.

articles.title_orig: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ is a cultural and economic earthquake. Brace yourself.
articles.title_zh: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ is a cultural and economic earthquake. Brace yourself.
articles.content_orig:
Grand Theft Auto VI protagonists, Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, against the backdrop of the Miami-inspired Vice City. Rockstar Games hide caption
I want to tell you about the time I saw Bigfoot. I want to tell you about sitting in the rain on a city street in a muscle car and prepping to rob a bank while lightning split the sky between high-rise condo towers in the distance and the drum fill from In The Air Tonight played on the radio. I want to tell you about gunfights and fistfights, the perfect satire of radio commercials and how the sunrise looks over Ocean Beach. But more than any of that, I want to tell you about the time an alligator bit my mom.
It happened in the backyard of an abandoned house with a rotting inground pool. My mom, Mia Caminos (mother of Lucia Caminos, one of the two leads in Rockstar Games' Grand Theft Auto VI , probably the most highly anticipated video game sequel of all time), was thrilled by the pool. Standing there, amid the artfully rendered weeds and trash, she spread her arms and told me to use my imagination, to see her vision for this ruin of a house with its upmarket water feature, in a scabby neighborhood on the outskirts of Vice City. She speaks in tones of increasingly frantic desperation because she has already put money down on this house, sight unseen. All of her money, actually, in hopes of flipping it and selling it fast to keep her startup real estate business afloat.
Lucia begins her epic as a petty criminal. Rockstar Games hide caption
The pool is still half full of water. There's a dirty, sodden mattress floating in it. And as if this is the main thing standing between her and success, Mia is fixated on getting it out of the pool.
Help me, Lucia , she says.
And, dutifully, I do. Playing as Lucia, I grab hold, mash buttons, help my mom drag away the wet, heavy, stinking mattress. And just as we get it up and over the lip of the pool that's going to be the thing that makes this wreck of a house suddenly desirable – that's when the alligator lunges out of the murky water, grabs my mom by the arm and tries to drag her back in.
This is a story about folly, fixation, unrealistic expectations of success at the ass-end of late capitalism, and the vicious, whip-crack cruelty of predators who lie in wait for anyone trying to improve a terrible situation.
But then I shoot the alligator in the head before it can eat my mom. Because this is also a story about violence, and how sometimes (maybe all the times), the loud, cathartic rip of gunfire is the only solution left for people who have already lost so much and can't bear to see one more thing taken from them.
It's a story about my mom and an alligator, sure.
It is also the story of GTA6
Grand Theft Auto VI returns to Vice City and its Florida-inspired environs. Rockstar Games hide caption
But let's back up a little. For anyone who has somehow missed the shrieking, neon-and-swamp-water marketing onslaught over the past several days, weeks, months and years, Grand Theft Auto VI is the newest release from Rockstar Games. It is a Bonnie and Clyde love story, a knife-edged satire of modern American culture and politics, an unapologetic murder simulator, a love letter to 50 years of crime movies, and a thoughtful, emotional meditation on the sacrifices, small and large, that we make for family. A massive open world game set in the fictional state of Leonida (based on the very real state of Florida), it represents a return to a location that Rockstar hasn't visited in-depth since its 2002 release of GTA: Vice City , and is the first new game in the franchise since GTA5 launched in 2013. According to estimates, it already earned over $1.5 billion in pre-sales and will likely make a total of $3 to $5 billion in its first week , which could make it the largest single entertainment product launch ever.
Fans have been waiting years for it. They have created libraries worth of lore and theories and dissected trailers frame-by-frame. To discount the overheated environment into which this singular work of art is being released would be doing a disservice both to it and the legions of salivating prognosticators who have made guessing the number of bird species included in-game , or speculating on the square mileage of its map, their entire personalities.
While Vice City remains the game's hub, most of its map is actually rural or wild. Rockstar Games hide caption
Now, though, they know it all. We all do. We know that GTA6 is expansive, covering everything from the Keys (where the game starts) to the hilly, forested north, with Vice City in all its grimy, pastel-colored splendor at the beating heart of it. It is a playground, equal parts gorgeous and maniacal, and in all that space the developers have given us a thousand different things to do. You can rob a bank or take a bike ride, go fishing, hunt trophy animals, visit strip clubs, rob random civilians, street race, fly drones, eat a sandwich, work out, manage your family savings account, jump a sports car off the top of a building, steal a plane, punch out a convenience store clerk, fight a bear or, yes, just wander out toward the horizon and study the birds. And while some of that is fun and all of it is diverting (at least for a little while), none of it is the ostensible point. The game-y part of the game — the hundred extras and time-wasters that players have come to expect from open-world projects in general, and GTA specifically — is not what makes it matter.
What matters is Mia and the alligator, Lucia and the gun. It's the multi-pronged, exquisitely balanced narrative about poverty and rigged systems that makes it hard to turn away from GTA while you're playing and impossible not to think about when you're away.
Jason and his pal, Cal, shoot pool. Rockstar Games hide caption
Lucia is an ex-con, a car thief and a small-time criminal who got caught trying to rob a payday loan joint and starts the game in jail. Her partner, Jason Duval, is a veteran, dishonorably discharged, now making a living flying loads for a local coke dealer down in the Keys and living rent-free in one of his properties. Jason skims a little on the coke deals, wears flip-flops and drinks beer in the sun, and goes fishing with his best friend Cal (played with genius-level goofy, drunken paranoia and dopey bravado by Bobby Moynihan). Jason and Lucia have a kid, Tomás, who is currently living with Lucia's family, and every plan they have is about getting right by the law, making a few bucks and grabbing a chance at finally being a family.
Only there are complications — surprisingly banal ones at first (like not being able to open a checking account because of their bad credit) — that slowly ramp up into huge ones across 60-odd hours of main story gameplay that see Jason and Lucia (both of whom are playable characters) graduate from knocking over liquor stores in a beat-up El Camino, to pulling off elaborate heists in the middle of Vice City which will have you dangling from a net suspended from a cargo helicopter hauling 200 tons of cocaine. It goes from Badlands to Die Hard with the speed of a muscle car, all bright chrome and barking straight pipes. From True Romance to Heat like that's just the natural arc of any American love story.
And what's remarkable about the whole bloody delight is that it remains, until its final operatic moments, so surprisingly grounded. This is a somewhat more mature GTA than its predecessors, trading aliens, cannibal cultists and whacked-out drug trips for wellness influencers, local politics and the music industry. Jason and Lucia's relationship is the superstructure around which the entire narrative is built, and it's a dynamic thing that must be maintained in a dozen little ways — making coffee in the morning, opening doors for each other, date nights (even if that means robbing a jewelry store together), or holding hands as you walk toward yet another betrayal by someone you thought you could trust. articles.title_orig: Waymo suspends all driverless taxi rides on freeways after ban in California
articles.title_zh: Waymo suspends all driverless taxi rides on freeways after ban in California
articles.content_orig:
Waymo has temporarily stopped offering driverless taxi rides on freeways after California banned the vehicles from state freeways following recent traffic incidents.
The company had allowed riders to hail its robotaxis for freeway rides in the San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, Phoenix, Miami and Austin. The California-based company offers rides on city streets in many other areas including Las Vegas, Dallas and Denver.
A Waymo spokesperson wrote in an email that the company has “temporarily restricted commercial freeway rides in all markets where we operate that service,” though it’s “continuing freeway testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel.” The suspension was implemented last Wednesday, according to the spokesperson, but they didn't say how long it would last.
Related video: Why are gas prices dropping and how low will they go?
The suspension came after the California Department of Motor Vehicles banned the company's robotaxis from freeways that same day. The ban followed two incidents including one in which three Waymo driverless vehicles drove into a construction zone, DMV spokesperson Jonathan Groveman said in a statement.
The construction zone incident occurred on Nov. 5 and the second incident, which involved California Highway Patrol vehicles, occurred the next day on a highway in San Francisco, according to Groveman.
Video of the Nov. 6 incident circulated widely on social media last week. In the footage, a Waymo vehicle can be seen trying to bypass California Highway Patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break.
“The Department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present,” Groveman said.
Groveman added that “similar incidents” previously occurred on May 18.
The Waymo spokesperson said the “recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California” did not “involve any injuries or collisions.”
California's restrictions bar Waymo from operating and testing its driverless vehicles on California freeways, according to Groveman. He said the restrictions will remain in effect until “Waymo demonstrates to the Department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions.”
Kelety reported from Phoenix.

articles.title_zh: Almost nobody’s vying for an invite to Trump’s second meme coin dinner
articles.content_orig:
Plus, high-stake negotiations are underway at the United Nations over killer robots, Palantir’s CEO is trying to rebrand his company as “progressive” and more — all in this week’s Tuesday Tech Drop.
Happy Tuesday! Here’s your Tuesday Tech Drop, some of the past week’s top stories from the intersection of politics and technology.
According to a new report from Reuters, the value of President Donald Trump ’s meme coin has cratered to record lows ahead of a cryptocurrency gala this weekend at his South Florida estate. The report also says that interest in the president’s third such gala “has collapsed.”
Rep. Robert Garcia, a California Democrat who is primed to become chair of the House Oversight Committee in January, told MS NOW that looking at Trump’s crypto ventures — and investors who may have felt legitimately scammed — will be a priority for his committee.
A federal judge has issued a permanent injunction barring the Justice Department or Department of Homeland Security from pressuring Apple to suppress Eyes Up, an app used for documenting immigration enforcement activity.
Read more at the Indiana Capital Chronicle .
As Trump continues to voice support for Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s CEO amid a scandal involving his affair with an alleged Chinese spy, scrutiny continues to mount over the president’s financial stake in the company behind some of the world’s most-coveted computer chips . My colleague Steve Benen wrote about recent reports on the timing and frequency with which Trump has traded Nvidia stock that raise even more questions.
High-stakes negotiations are underway at the United Nations as representatives gather this week to discuss potential regulations on lethal autonomous weapons.
Palantir CEO Alex Karp, whose tech firm has been central to Trump’s racist anti-immigrant crackdown , is trying to rebrand his company as “progressive” after Democrats’ blue wave in the midterms.
Trump has invested in several of the companies that his transportation secretary wants to build a multibillion-dollar network for the Federal Aviation Administration after last week’s nationwide ground stop debacle, and I wrote about the president’s financial entanglements.
An Army major and whistleblower said Pentagon leaders shrugged off warnings about the need for adequate protection before an Iranian drone strike killed six U.S. service members. Trump responded by raging at CBS News’ “60 Minutes” for airing the claims — without disputing their merits.
Lauren Chen, a right-wing influencer who has been accused of being paid by the Russian government to peddle pro-Kremlin propaganda to American audiences, made a recent appearance at the president’s Mar-a-Lago property in Florida.
Read more at The New Republic.
After making history by winning his Senate race in Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom still has questions about how his state used inaccurate data from Experian to mark some voters as inactive ahead of this year’s midterms. Now, Mississippi’s Republican secretary of state is warring with the credit reporting company as those questions swirl.
Read more at Democracy Docket .

articles.title_orig: Trump arrives in China ahead of high-stakes talks with Xi, Putin amid US technical outages
articles.title_zh: Trump arrives in China ahead of high-stakes talks with Xi, Putin amid US technical outages
articles.content_orig:
by ALEXX ALTMAN-DEVILBISS | The National News Desk
CHINA (TNND)  — President Donald Trump arrived in China on Wednesday ahead of a high-stakes trilateral meeting Thursday with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The trip comes as Trump seeks to strengthen the United States’ position as a global technology leader, while a series of technical outages has fueled speculation about possible cyberattacks.
After additional outages were reported Tuesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sought to reassure Americans Wednesday, saying there was “zero” evidence the disruptions were connected or linked to rival nations, hackers or criminals.
“Sometimes when you are going in to fix your system because you’ve identified a vulnerability, it creates a short-term disruption,” said Rubio, who also serves as Trump’s national security adviser.
Outages reported since Friday have affected Microsoft , the Federal Aviation Administration , JPMorgan Chase and the National Security Agency's communications network.
In Shenzhen, China’s technology hub and the host city for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, Xi greeted Trump on the tarmac in a gesture that reciprocated Trump’s welcome during Xi’s September visit to Washington. Putin, who arrived earlier Wednesday, was not greeted at the airport. The two leaders later shook hands before an APEC group photo.
Trump has signaled he wants to rely on informal, relationship-based diplomacy during the trip. He said he plans to discuss nuclear weapons and the war in Ukraine with Xi and Putin, though his aides had previously said Ukraine would not be on the agenda. Analysts have tempered expectations for a breakthrough.
Trump also said he may meet privately with Putin and separately with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un , though neither meeting was on his official schedule. On Wednesday, he was also set to meet with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, amid his criticism of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade agreement.
The talks are unfolding amid broader tensions over super intelligence and advanced computer chips. The rapid development of SI offers the prospect of economic growth but also raises national security concerns. Trump has said there are differences within his administration over restricting China’s access to advanced chips, adding, “We have a very good relationship with China, and you don’t want to insult them.”
Before arriving in China, Trump met with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in Manila and said the countries had reached a trade deal. He also briefly reunited with Marcos’ mother, former first lady Imelda Marcos, whom he has known for decades.
Trump said on Truth Social that the leaders had a "wonderful meeting on Trade, National Security, and other subjects."
"I am pleased to announce that we made a new and completely different Trade Deal with the Philippines, one that will be a true landmark and, in particular, a Deal that will be great for our Farmers and those in the business of 'Energy,' Trump wrote. "President Marcos is a powerful leader, and a man of high integrity and substance. It was an Honor to be with him, and his beautiful wife and son."

articles.title_orig: Fed’s Waller says central bank may need to ‘shock people’ with half-point rate hike
articles.title_zh: Fed’s Waller says central bank may need to ‘shock people’ with half-point rate hike
articles.content_orig:
Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller on Wednesday called for aggressive action against inflation , saying the central bank need to "shock people" as prices continue to rise more than he expected.
In the near term, the policymaker told CNBC in a live interview that a half-percentage-point increase in the Fed's benchmark rate is probably necessary at the Dec. 8-9 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee.
He said the Fed needs to reverse the three quarter-point reductions from last year and may need to do more.
"I'm very, very concerned about inflation. It's kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it's spreading out," Waller told CNBC's Steve Liesman during a "Squawk Box" interview. "If you really want to get it down, you've got to start taking more aggressive actions."
"You might need to, like, shock people," he said.
Futures prices are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point hike at the FOMC's Dec. 8-9 meeting. They also are anticipating another move in January, followed by at least one additional increase before the end of 2027, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge.
Waller said the Fed wouldn't necessarily have to approve a half-point hike in December if it raised rates by a quarter point and signaled another move coming in January. However, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has been against that kind of forward guidance on grounds that it ties policymakers' hands.
"If you're not going to signal this very clearly to markets, you're going in January, my view is then you have to go 50 [basis points] in December to put it in place and get it done," he said.
Recent statements from other central bankers indicate a range of opinions , though most agree that more policy tightening is needed to bring down inflation.
In a speech Tuesday, St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem suggested as many as four hikes by the spring of 2027. Some Fed officials, including regional presidents Beth Hammack of Cleveland and Lorie Logan of Dallas, have endorsed more gradual tightening.
However, continued inflation above the Fed's 2% target might push officials into a more aggressive stance.
The FOMC approved its first interest rate hike in more than three years in September, and then held rates steady at its October meeting. While inflation has continued to run hot since then, other Fed officials seem less eager to drop the policy hammer as heavily as Waller.
"I don't think the situation calls for dramatic action," New York Fed President John Williams said Tuesday in a conversation with Axios. "I think what we've been doing over the last past few months is ... working well. We're collecting the data, analyzing it, having the debate and making a decision."
The Fed in 2025 approved three rate cuts amid worries over the labor market and the belief that inflation would continue to moderate toward the central bank's 2% goal.
However, inflation reignited earlier this year after the strikes the U.S. and Israel launched against Iran in late February. Energy prices spiked while tariff impacts lingered, keeping most inflation readings above 3% .
"First of all, you've got to take back the three insurance cuts we put in last year," Waller said. "If the policy rate last summer in 2025 wasn't bringing inflation down, getting back to that isn't going to bring it down. So we may have to go above ... three hikes plus maybe some more to get it to start actually coming back down."
The FOMC later Wednesday will release minutes from the October meeting.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street prepares for Anthropic IPO frenzy, despite broader AI stock slump
articles.title_zh: Wall Street prepares for Anthropic IPO frenzy, despite broader AI stock slump
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
As Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) prepares to begin trading under the ticker ANT on Thursday, Nov. 19, business leaders are weighing in on the historically large initial public offering (IPO).
"There's no difference in investing in Anthropic on the IPO than Amazon on its IPO," "Shark Tank" host and O'Leary Ventures chair Kevin O'Leary said on Sozzi Unleashed . "There was tremendous volatility. It made zero money. But look at the platform it ultimately built. That's what you're betting on in the Anthropic deal."
Sitting down with Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi, O'Leary said the past few years haven't been great for buying IPOs, but he believes Anthropic may be a unique way to bet on artificial intelligence.
Anthropic said it expects to sell 825 million shares priced between $70 and $78 each. That would give the company a market valuation of between $1.3 trillion and $1.45 trillion — putting it near SpaceX's ( SPCX ) IPO valuation of $1.77 trillion, which was the largest ever.
Read more: Everything you need to know ahead of Anthropic's IPO
"It may be the most hyped IPO ever," O'Leary said. "This IPO is the anchor to the entire AI or SI trade, whatever you want to call it."
What about the fact that Anthropic may not turn a profit until 2030? Though Anthropic's operating losses have improved, they still total $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year. The company also noted in its amended IPO filing that it plans to spend nearly $900 billion on computing and data centers, with $70 billion of that total coming due within a year.
O'Leary said Anthropic's profitability is the wrong lens right now. Buying in is a bet on AI's role across all 11 sectors of the economy, and he sees evidence of productivity and margin gains so far. That has helped markets remain near all-time highs despite tariffs, wars, and high energy prices.
These remarks follow O'Leary's comments last month, when the businessman called Anthropic "a hot trade."
"I expect it to be liquid from day one, and that changes the opportunity," he wrote in October.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia stops shipping US-approved AI chips to China
articles.title_zh: Nvidia stops shipping US-approved AI chips to China
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, acting CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday, ending the company's participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country.
China's access to leading AI accelerators was an important topic during the company's first earnings call since CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down last week. The disclosure comes the same day Nvidia announced it was creating a board-level committee to oversee national security policies , export control compliance, and global trade risks.
Nvidia's deal to sell H200 chips in China was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump. The arrangement required the chips to be shipped through the U.S., allowing the government to collect a 25% tariff.
The pathway angered China hawks who wanted to deny Chinese labs computing power and maintain the United States' lead in AI, but Huang long argued that it was more important for the U.S. to compete in China. In April, he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that "to concede that market for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country."
Huang's ouster — in part over an affair with the CEO of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China — has coincided with new rules, issued Monday, barring advanced U.S. chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely.
Investment bank Jefferies forecast that those rules might trim between $44 billion and $62 billion from Nvidia's data center revenue next year. Referencing the new export controls, Kress said that the backlog of demand for advanced chips like Vera Rubin means the rules would have no impact on the company's top-line revenue.
In the long term, the company may face the loss of potential customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Critics of Nvidia's dependence on China claim that as much as 20% of its revenue comes from demand linked to the country — annual revenue at its Singapore subsidiary hit $104 billion in 2025 before Nvidia stopped disclosing those figures — but that's clearly going to change.
Even before Nvidia decided to stop shipping H200s, China had largely refused to accept their delivery. The government would prefer to generate demand for the country's domestic chip industry, even if major AI compute users want the still-superior Nvidia equipment, according to Jacob Feldgoise, a researcher at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology.
Meanwhile, Chinese frontier labs are finding ways to access Nvidia chips elsewhere. All of China's leading AI models show evidence of having been trained on Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips that are prohibited from being exported to China.
That training may have taken place at data centers outside of China, but sales to those facilities will be barred under the new rules. If large data centers suited for training AI models want to buy Nvidia chips, they will have to certify they aren't serving any Chinese customers, export control attorney Dan Fisher-Owens told TechCrunch.
If they can't provide that certification, the new rules may force them toward other chip options and further eat into Nvidia's market share.

articles.title_orig: In Choosing Shenzhen for Trump-Putin Summit, Xi Shows Off His Tech Ambitions
articles.title_zh: In Choosing Shenzhen for Trump-Putin Summit, Xi Shows Off His Tech Ambitions
articles.content_orig:
Host city offers showcase of China’s rise into a confident and innovative power central to global economy
I n a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping , is basking in its neon glow.
On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage.
The broader Apec summit , meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US.
All this is set against the futuristic backdrop that is Shenzhen, a city that perhaps better than no other embodies China’s rise into a confident, technologically innovative power central to the global economy.
A photo display in the Apec media centre charts Shenzhen’s transformation from sparsely populated marshland, calling it “a miracle in the history of world development created by the Chinese people”.
“[Xi] wants people to go home Chinamaxxing,” said Prof Astrid Nordin, of King’s College London. “Shenzhen is itself part of the message. It’s a showcase of Chinese technological and economic achievements, and of China’s claim that it offers opportunities for prosperity in a world increasingly characterised by uncertainty and conflict.”
Like the light show, the summit is being carefully coordinated. The Financial Times cited people familiar with the matter as saying it would be one of the most tightly controlled in the organisation’s history, with leaders having to travel to a state guesthouse beside Shenzhen’s tiger safari park to meet Xi. The paper said diplomats had grumbled that the format “seems designed to reduce the free-flowing discussion characteristic of prior editions”.
Setting out its expectations for the summit, China’s foreign ministry has said it looks forward to “practical results in key areas such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, AI and so on”.
Already, Xi has announced trade wins with Canada’s Mark Carney, extending remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.
A meeting with Papua New ⁠Guinea’s leader, meanwhile, showed how Beijing’s geopolitical priorities have been absorbed and reflected by its allies, with James Marape recounting to Xi how he had closed Taiwan’s office in his country despite domestic challenges in doing so.
The most important meeting will be between Xi and Trump. The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are expected to tackle a broad range of issues including AI and trade. In a move that could strain the fragile tariff truce that the two leaders first agreed last year, the Trump administration said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips.
Christopher Adams, a senior adviser at the law firm Covington who was at the centre of trade negotiations with China for the Obama and first Trump administrations, said: “The trade truce may increasingly look like a ceasefire in a war where major combat operations remain on hold but skirmishes are escalating to the point where the line between peace and war is blurred.
“I don’t see pressure to announce a further extension of the trade truce in Shenzhen. If a significant extension is announced, that would be an upside surprise.”
China has not hesitated to leverage Apec’s multinational platform in service of its arguments. A commentary by the state news agency Xinhua on Tuesday said: “Amid deepening geopolitical rivalries and growing global divisions, [China’s hosting] sends a clear signal that great-power competition need not be a zero-sum game, and that one country’s development need not come at the expense of another.”
The chair of the Apec senior officials’ meeting, Chen Xu, said Beijing had made trade “openness” a key focus of its Apec year and looked forward to “achieving more practical outcomes on the trade front”.
The much anticipated trilateral summit with Trump and Putin, on the other hand, could prove largely symbolic. For Xi, “it provides the appearance of China shaping the world order as an equal to the United States,” said Dr Kevork Oskanian, an expert on Russia at the University of Exeter. “Agreement on substantial issues, which would, in any case, require extensive preparatory negotiations, is unlikely.”
For China’s ruling Communist party, the political pomp has another key purpose. Nordin said summits were “occasions for leaders to tell stories about the world, about their country’s place in it … and one of the most important audiences for those stories is at home.”
For the locals watching the skyscraper light show on Monday night, the symbolism was not lost. China’s export might had helped it become increasingly powerful on the world stage, said one local man, who did not give his name. “It’s so great that the summit will take place in Shenzhen,” he said. “I feel very proud.”

(Kitco NewsWire) - Spot gold prices were little changed in late U.S. trading Tuesday, while silver rebounded from Monday's sharp losses as weaker U.S. economic data, declining Treasury yields and renewed geopolitical tensions competed with expectations for additional Federal Reserve tightening. Gold struggled to sustain gains despite a weaker dollar and another broad equity market selloff, while silver attracted bargain hunting after its recent decline. Spot gold was trading near $3,853.10 an ounce, down $2.40, or 0.06%, while spot silver was trading near $47.330, up $0.472, or 1.01%, on the session. Gold traded between $3,836.00 and $3,891.60 during the day, while silver's range extended from approximately $46.710 to $48.130.
Tuesday's U.S. economic reports provided further evidence of uneven growth as elevated borrowing costs and persistent inflation continued to pressure consumers and industrial activity. October retail sales increased 0.2%, matching expectations but slowing substantially from September's 0.8% advance. Sales excluding automobiles rose 0.6%, above expectations for a 0.4% increase, suggesting underlying spending remained comparatively resilient. Industrial production declined 0.4% in October, substantially below expectations for a 0.1% increase, following September's 0.7% gain. Manufacturing output increased 0.3%, while mining production fell 0.8% and utilities output declined 4.3%. Capacity utilization slipped to 76.4%. The mixed figures reinforced concerns about slowing economic momentum without providing sufficient evidence that inflation pressures have eased enough to alter the Fed's tightening trajectory.
Market positioning remained heavily tilted toward another Federal Reserve interest rate increase at the Dec. 8-9 policy meeting. The latest published futures assessments indicated approximately a 94% probability of a 25-basis-point increase, with the remaining 6% favoring a larger 50-basis-point move. Those expectations followed stronger October employment and inflation figures, although Tuesday's weaker industrial production report and renewed equity selling encouraged demand for Treasury securities. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield eased toward 5.10% in late trading, while the two-year yield declined toward 4.79%. The dollar also retreated from recent highs, providing some support to precious metals. Investors now turn to Wednesday's October housing starts and building permits figures at 8:30 a.m. EST, followed by the minutes of the Fed's Oct. 27-28 meeting at 2 p.m. EST. Nvidia's upcoming earnings and additional Fed commentary could also influence risk sentiment, Treasury yields and expectations for December policy.
The Strait of Hormuz and U.S.-Iran situation deteriorated Tuesday as additional military incidents and tanker attacks intensified concerns about the security of commercial shipping through the strategic waterway. Iranian drones attacked a U.S. military radar installation in Bahrain, while U.S. forces carried out retaliatory strikes against a missile-launch site on Iran's Qeshm Island. The crew of a vessel struck twice in the Strait of Hormuz was also unaccounted for, adding to concerns about maritime safety. Shipping activity had already slowed considerably following attacks on tankers operated by the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company, with vessel-tracking figures indicating only five commodity vessels transited the strait Saturday, compared with 31 during the preceding weekend, and none recorded Sunday. U.S.-Iran diplomatic efforts remained stalled, leaving the risk of further escalation elevated. The renewed hostilities supported crude oil prices and maintained a geopolitical risk premium in gold, although expectations for restrictive U.S. monetary policy and broader financial-market liquidation continued to limit bullion's response.
Crude oil futures recovered modestly Tuesday as renewed risks to Persian Gulf shipping and expectations for declining U.S. inventories supported prices following Monday's sharp decline. Brent crude futures settled $0.70 higher, or 0.76%, at $93.14 a barrel, while Nymex WTI advanced $0.29, or 0.34%, to $86.01. The rebound remained limited by expectations for recovering Middle Eastern exports and an emerging global petroleum surplus. Brent has declined approximately 20% during November, while WTI has fallen about 16%, reflecting the substantial unwinding of earlier geopolitical supply premiums. For gold, renewed energy-price pressure presents conflicting implications: military escalation can increase defensive demand, while sustained petroleum-driven inflation could reinforce expectations for higher interest rates and restrict precious metals' upside.
North American equity markets finished sharply lower Tuesday, extending Monday's technology-led selloff as concerns about artificial intelligence valuations, export restrictions and corporate earnings weighed on investor sentiment. The Dow Jones Industrial Average declined approximately 849 points, or 1.6%, to close at 50,759.42, while the S&P 500 lost 1.0% to finish at 7,340.53. The Nasdaq Composite fell 0.7% to 24,328.38, and the Russell 2000 declined 1.5% to 2,701.87. Semiconductor and technology shares remained volatile ahead of Nvidia's earnings, while financial stocks also contributed to the broader retreat. The continued decline encouraged demand for government bonds, although gold's limited response suggested that defensive buying was being offset by position reductions and persistent monetary tightening expectations.
Canada's S&P/TSX Composite Index also traded lower Tuesday, extending Monday's 1.06% decline as technology shares and broader weakness in risk assets weighed on the Toronto market. The index was down approximately 0.74% near 35,456 during the afternoon, compared with Monday's confirmed close of 35,722.13. Weakness in selected growth-oriented companies reflected the broader deterioration in North American sentiment, while precious metals producers faced a mixed underlying commodity market as gold remained subdued and silver recovered. Energy shares received some support from the rebound in crude oil. A confirmed Tuesday closing value for the Canadian benchmark was not available in the verified market figures used for this report.
European equity markets finished sharply lower Tuesday, extending the global retreat as technology shares and financial companies came under renewed selling pressure. The pan-European Stoxx 600 declined 1.75% to close at 650.72, while Germany's DAX fell 2.08% to 26,045.37. France's CAC 40 lost 1.62% to 8,216.78, and the U.K.'s FTSE 100 declined 1.76% to 10,689.87. Semiconductor equipment companies remained under pressure following tighter U.S. restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence chip exports to China, while weakness in European banks contributed to the broader decline. Energy and telecommunications shares demonstrated relative resilience, reflecting stronger crude oil prices and defensive sector rotation.
The key outside markets see Nymex WTI crude oil futures higher after settling at $86.01 a barrel, while Brent crude finished at $93.14. The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield eased toward 5.10%, while the two-year yield declined near 4.79%. articles.title_orig: Iran widens Gulf attacks, targeting US air base in Kuwait and sites in Bahrain
articles.title_zh: Iran widens Gulf attacks, targeting US air base in Kuwait and sites in Bahrain
articles.content_orig:
Iran said its army targeted U.S. drone and missile installations at Kuwait's Ali Al Salem air base, according to local media , extending a series of attacks on Gulf states hosting American forces.
Kuwait's army said on Tuesday evening that its air defenses had countered hostile drone attacks, without providing further details.
Tensions between Iran and the U.S. have escalated sharply in recent days as strikes resumed across the Middle East, even as diplomatic talks continued.
Bahrain has also sustained a wave of Iranian drone strikes , issuing an "all-clear" alert on Wednesday after its air defenses intercepted several aerial threats. Iran has previously claimed attacks on U.S. radar systems in Bahrain.
CNN reported late Monday that U.S. intelligence found Iran was developing plans that could involve a so-called dirty bomb to target Washington, D.C. The administration officials, including President Donald Trump, have played down any imminent threat while saying the government continues to monitor the situation.
Speaking at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila, Philippines, Trump warned that Iran would "pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before" if such a plan existed.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio echoed Trump's comments when addressing reporters in Manila, saying he did not see any imminent threats to the U.S. capital, but that the government is "always on the lookout for anything that's a threat."
Trump nodded and said, "We are looking into it," while adding, "We are doing very well in Iran."
The renewed attacks come as diplomatic efforts to end the U.S.-Israel war with Iran, now in its ninth month, appear to be stalled, while disruptions continue to weigh on energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
Crude futures settled lower amid signs of recovering oil flows through the critical waterway. The International Energy Agency said Friday that the global oil supply had surpassed demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war and projected the market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter.
The U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures dropped 1.2% to $84.9 a barrel, while Brent was down 0.48% at $92.7 per barrel.

articles.title_zh: Grand Theft Auto VI Uses AMD FSR 4 On Xbox Series S, Upscaling 720p To 1080p While Still Running Ray Traced Global Illumination
articles.content_orig:
During Grand Theft Auto VI 's review period , Rockstar Games offered us the chance to send some questions to the developers. Being a tech-focused website, there was a lot we wanted to know about the studio's design goals for this iteration of the RAGE engine .
Did they try to achieve a frame rate higher than 30 frames per second ? What were the rendering resolutions for each system? What kind of challenges did adding ray traced global illumination present, and what was their approach to HDR support?
All of these questions are answered below in a lengthy statement crafted by Jonathon Ashcroft - Senior Vice President of Technology, Chris Oat – Technical Director: Engine and Graphics, and Marc Chambers – Technology Production Director.
It became clear early on that given the scale of the team’s ambition, we’d be targeting 30fps on this generation of hardware. We’ve put a lot of effort into balancing presentation, simulation, and gameplay, as well as ensuring the input latency is vastly improved vs. Grand Theft Auto V and Red Dead Redemption 2. Part of that process was determining our base resolution and upscaling solution. We evaluated a variety of approaches for each console, then selected a combination of each that gave us the look and performance we needed.
On all platforms, the picture is then composited with a 4K UI and presented. For each console, we’ve arrived at our solution through careful evaluation of both the visuals and the performance.  We built our core lighting, frame processing, and final presentation pipeline with both HDR and SDR support in mind from the outset. We calibrated our engine’s in-game light sources according to the real-world physical properties of natural and artificial light sources.
We also built a new physically-based material library used to represent every material type you will see in game. From the way muddy alligator skin glistens in the Leonida sunshine, to the way hair and clothing reacts to the dynamic light shows in a nightclub, and the complex lighting interactions of exotic vehicle paint zipping under highway street lights — it was all built to behave according the physical laws of light. Finally, that rendered frame goes through an imaging pipeline modelled after real word cinematic camera and film treatment, much like you would expect of a modern movie. The aim is always to try and create and preserve emersion for the player, so they can experience it as the team imagined it, whether they are experiencing the game in HDR or SDR.
This focus on lighting made it vital for us to ensure we could use the same lighting solution on each console, including the Xbox Series S, where memory pressure posed a bit of a challenge. The results made that a challenge worth overcoming. There are indeed some differences between the implementations per console, as we rebalance the RTGI features to achieve the best presentation based on each platform’s capabilities. As with everything, we tune on a given piece of hardware to achieve the presentation we’re looking for, so there’s no single solution.
I also asked Rockstar a couple of more artistic questions, which were answered separately by the studio's VP of Art, Michael Kane . You can find them below.
The game's corners of the screen often seem a little darkened, kind of like a vignette effect. Can you confirm that's the case? If so, would it be possible to add it as a toggle option for those who dislike it?
Michael Kane, Vice President of Art: Dynamic: The vignette effect is an artistic choice. We currently do not support any toggle, but we have recently identified and fixed an issue where it was becoming stronger than intended in certain circumstances.
In key Grand Theft Auto VI artworks, Jason looks very different from the in-game character, whereas Lucia looks much closer. How did your design for each character evolve through development, and did you have any specific references or inspirations that you can share?
Michael Kane, Vice President of Art: Dynamic: There could typically be a perceptual interpretation of the key art versus in-game, especially for Jason… because both of them are so customizable, we think many players will maybe want ‘their Jason’ to have a mustache or long hair in a certain style or colour etc when they play. So far, we’ve only seen those more diverse looks on him in screenshots and not key marketing art, so that’s the best anchor point for our intention for him – that’s his ground truth, in-game.
About the author : With over two decades of experience in gaming journalism, Alessio Palumbo has led the gaming vertical at Wccftech since August 2015. He started working at a young age for Italian websites like Everyeye.it, Gamestar.it, Nextgame.it, and Multiplayer.it before kickstarting the indie English-language publication Worlds Factory as its founder and Editor in Chief. 

In the last decade, he has coordinated the overall output of Wccftech's gaming section, managed PR relations, assigned reviews, produced daily news coverage, edited gaming content as needed, and delivered game reviews.  

Arguably, his trademark content is the long series of exclusive developer interviews that have been cited by Wikipedia and by the biggest news media and gaming publications. 

His passion for technology also makes him knowledgeable when it comes to gaming hardware and tech. His favorite genres include RPGs, MMORPGs, and action/adventure games.
Follow Wccftech on Google to get more of our news coverage in your feeds.

articles.title_orig: Putin Arrives in Asia With a Show of Force: Nuclear Bombers
articles.title_zh: Putin Arrives in Asia With a Show of Force: Nuclear Bombers
articles.content_orig:
Japan says it launched fighter jets and "strongly" protested after two suspected Russian aircraft violated its airspace early on Tuesday.
South Korea also says it deployed fighter jets, while Taiwan says it "responded" to Russian military aircraft detected in their respective air defence identification zones.
These are unofficial buffer areas beyond territorial airspace where governments identify approaching aircraft for security purposes. Moscow has yet to comment.
The alleged incursions are a reminder of Russia's military power ahead of the Apec economic summit in China this week, which Vladimir Putin will attend alongside US President Donald Trump.
Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the flight paths of the Russian aircraft, off the south-western Okinoshima island, were a "serious infringement of Japan's sovereignty" and "completely unacceptable".
The last such incursion was in 2024, when a Russian military patrol plane entered Japanese airspace off Rebun island, Hokkaido.
Taiwan says its military "responded accordingly" after two Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone, also on Tuesday.
South Korea says it sent up jets after an unspecified number of Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone over the Sea of Japan. The aircraft departed without violating South Korean airspace, authorities said.
It is unclear if the three neighbours were responding to the same or different aircraft.
The East China Sea contains self-declared, overlapping air defence identification zones between China, Taiwan, Japan and South Korea.
Foreign military aircraft are expected, but not legally required, to notify governments before entering such air defence identification zones.
Tensions are flaring between Japan and Russia, which are locked in a decades-old territorial dispute over a cluster of islands in the Pacific Ocean.
For months, Moscow has been ratcheting up the pressure on Tokyo.
In August, Putin paid his first visit to one of these islands, prompting sharp rebuke from Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. In October, Russia detained a Japanese journalist on spying allegations.

articles.title_orig: Steve Rosenberg: Historic talks with Xi and Trump are a coup for Putin
articles.title_zh: Steve Rosenberg: Historic talks with Xi and Trump are a coup for Putin
articles.content_orig:
The meeting hasn't even happened yet.
But Thursday's mini summit of Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping already looks like a win for the Kremlin.
Think back to 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine President Putin was an international pariah. Western leaders were determined to isolate him and his country over the war in Ukraine.
Fast forward to 2026: Vladimir Putin has secured an historic meeting in Shenzhen. For the first time in history, the leaders of China, Russia and the United States will sit down – just the three of them – for talks.
That puts Putin exactly where he wants to be: at the top table of global politics, rubbing shoulders with the leaders of the two great powers.
It allows him to boast that Western pressure on Russia has failed.
"We see such examples in the failed attempts to isolate our country, Russia, which has faced unprecedented sanctions pressure," Putin told a business forum of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation organisation.
That was followed by a meeting with Xi Jinping.
But the Kremlin says the "showstopper" event in Shenzhen will be Putin's trilateral with Xi and Trump.
It allows him to play global statesman, even as the Russian military continues to pound Ukrainian towns and cities, and the Kremlin continues to reject the idea of an unconditional, comprehensive ceasefire.
One short meeting is unlikely to reshape the world. But it's the optics that are key. The picture. The photo-op. Three leaders, three big powers, discussing big issues.
In a way, Vladimir Putin will use this meeting to send a holiday postcard to the rest of the world. Instead of "Wish you were here", he'll sign it: "Look: I'm here."
But what of those who are not at the table?
Among European leaders, and especially in Ukraine, there is concern that the three-way meeting might produce more than just a pretty picture, though not in a good way for Kyiv.
Donald Trump has already said that in Shenzhen he wants to discuss his "favourite subject" - the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin would likely welcome an opportunity to argue its case to Trump and Xi without Ukrainian officials or European leaders in the room.
Last month Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed concern that the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting might resemble the Yalta Conference of 1945. That is when the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the United States – Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt - met to re-organise post-World War Two Europe.
"We really don't want this to turn into 'Yalta 2, 3, 4' with a redistribution of influence," said Zelensky.
It is unclear whether China would want the Ukraine war on the agenda in Shenzhen. In its official statements on the upcoming trilateral meeting, Beijing has talked more generally about the need to discuss "safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability".
In Shenzhen, Russia will make the most of the optics. But a diplomatic victory is not the same as a military one.
Nearly five years after President Putin launched his so-called "special military operation", Russia is still struggling to win its war on Ukraine.
Over this time, it has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.
And the Ukrainian strike on the road bridge linking Russia to the Crimean Peninsula – carried out on the eve of the summit - was a blow to Moscow's prestige. The attack severely damaged part of the multi-billion-dollar bridge built by Russia after it annexed Crimea from Ukraine.
The damage is not only a logistical headache for the Russian authorities.
It is a reminder that the Kremlin's "special operation" has not gone at all to plan.
The Shenzhen summit may give Vladimir Putin a big stage, and a bright spotlight.
It does not necessarily bring him closer to winning the war.

articles.title_orig: Stock futures rise as Nvidia gains on earnings beat and solid outlook: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures rise as Nvidia gains on earnings beat and solid outlook: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures climbed Wednesday morning after the S&P 500 fell for a fourth straight day. Traders also weighed Nvidia 's better-than-expected earnings report.
Nasdaq-100 futures were up 1%, while S&P 500 futures added 0.58%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were up 0.32%.
Shares of Nvidia were almost 3% higher in premarket trade, after jumping 4% in extended trading after the company's profit and revenue in the third quarter beat analysts' estimates. The company also lifted its revenue guidance for the fiscal year ending January 2028, calling for 75% growth year over year.
"The fact that they gave guidance is huge," said Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, on CNBC's "Closing Bell: Overtime. " " That is a very bullish sign. I expect the stock to move higher based just on that alone."
Neocloud companies also rose in extended trading. CoreWeave advanced 8%, while Nebius Group gained 10%.
During the regular trading day, the Dow dropped 1.6%. The S&P 500 slipped 1% and notched its lowest closing level since July 29, while the Nasdaq Composite shed 0.7%. During the day, the tech-heavy index touched its lowest level since April.
Looking ahead, traders are awaiting building permits and housing starts data. The Federal Open Market Committee's minutes from its October meeting will also be out in the afternoon. Federal Reserve policymakers last month decided to keep the overnight funds rate in a range of 3.75% to 4%.
On the earnings front, Lowe's, Target and TJ Maxx-parent TJX Cos are slated to report Wednesday morning.
Later this week, investors are awaiting a blockbuster initial public offering from Anthropic. The AI giant's shares are expected to be priced above the current range between $70 and $78, multiple sources told CNBC's David Faber on Tuesday.
Across the Atlantic, stock markets were mixed on Wednesday, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 hovering just below the flatline in morning trade. The U.K.'s FTSE 100 was 0.34% down, with France's CAC 40 sliding almost 0.1%, but Germany's DAX advanced 0.15%.
Most Asian markets closed in positive territory after a choppy trading session. South Korea's Kospi led gains in the region as chip heavyweights gained ground, ending 1.99% higher at 5,067.44, while Japan's Nikkei 225 gained 0.28% to close at 59,024.28,
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was 0.87% lower in its final hour of trade, while the CSI 300 on mainland China advanced 0.18% to 3,983.77. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 slipped 0.69%, marking a fifth straight day of losses.
Richard Reyle, chief investment officer at New Jersey-based Questar Capital Partners, said in a note Wednesday that Nvidia is "uninvestable."
"Nvidia is the Jenga tower of the whole AI trade, and that is not a compliment," he said. "A week ago, we thought this was a pedestrian story about a CEO whose ego got the best of him. Then we found out there was no clear succession plan, and poor corporate governance, with no Chairman until this scandal came to light."
He added that Nvidia's delayed 10-Q was a "red flag, as it's out of character from its previous releases."
"We believe there are significant questions about where Nvidia has been selling its chips," Reyle said. "For investors who own the stock, this is an immediate sell in our view. We have never owned Nvidia and believe the stock has been and remains uninvestable."
Shares of Nvidia were up around 4% in pre-market trading on Wednesday.
"There's another company set to begin a spectacular run (Anthropic), and every moment spent worrying about Nvidia is time that could have been spent finding the next winner," Reyle added. "News flash: NVDA ain't it."
Nvidia stock was up nearly 4% in premarket trading on Wednesday after reporting another earnings beat , as the fallout from CEO Jensen Huang's resignation continues to unfold.
The chip giant's stock was 3.96% higher at 5.08 a.m. ET on Wednesday in pre-market trading.
Neoclouds were buoyed by the results. CoreWeave was up 6.2%, Nebius 8.1% and Iren 7.4%.
U.S.-listed semiconductor stocks rose in pre-market trading Wednesday, following Nvidia's earnings beat.
Ahead of the opening bell, Nvidia stock was trading 3.9% higher, with the iShares and VanEck semiconductor ETFs both adding around 2.8%.
Marvell Technology added 4.3%, Arm was up by 3.8% and Micron gained 3.6%. KLA Corporation and AMD also traded more than 3% higher.
President Donald Trump has landed in China for the APEC summit, where he is due to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in the first trilateral talks between the three leaders on Thursday.
The meeting — taking place in Shenzhen, a major tech hub — puts trade and technology in sharp focus. Markets will be watching for any sign of progress on U.S.-China trade tensions or restrictions on advanced AI chips.
Xi opened the summit by calling for fewer trade and investment barriers and closer cooperation on artificial intelligence.
Traders are also watching for any signal on Ukraine, sanctions and energy, and the conflict in the Middle East , which could shape expectations for Russian oil exports and the geopolitical risk premium.
Precious metals sold off Wednesday morning, with gold falling to its lowest level in over a year and silver also plunging to a 52-week low, as expectations of interest rate rises from the Federal Reserve next month drew investors away from non-interest bearing assets.
Gold futures fell 2.34% to $3,761.84, while spot gold was down 2.38% at $3,758%. Silver futures slipped 3.5% to $45.72, as spot silver shed 3.6% to reach $45.67.
Nannette Hechler-Fayd'herbe, Lombard Odier Group's chief investment officer for EMEA and head of investment strategy, sustainability and research, said she remained optimistic on gold over the next 12 months, but warned that investors may need to be patient.
Hechler-Fayd'herbe does not expect the Federal Reserve or other central banks to embark on a sustained series of interest-rate hikes. But with U.S. real yields moving back up to 2.9%, from 2.6% not long ago, conditions are not yet supportive of an immediate rally, she said.
"This of course is not an environment where gold can immediately perform, so a little bit of patience on gold I think is warranted," she told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" Wednesday.
European stock markets were largely negative in early trading on Wednesday, with the Stoxx 600 edging just below the flatline shortly after 8:00 a.m. in London (3:00 a.m. E.T.).
Technology stocks advanced 1.16%, leading continental sectors, while industrial goods added 0.19%. But most other sectors were in the red, with basic resources tumbling 2.41%, while autos fell 0.43%.
Germany's DAX was up almost 0.1% in early trading in Frankfurt.
The U.K.'s FTSE 100 was down 0.32% in London, while in Paris, the CAC 40 was flat.  In Milan, the Italian FTSE MIB was hovering just below the flatline.
Indonesia's central bank on Wednesday raised rates by 25 basis points in a surprise move, bringing its policy rate to 6% — last seen in December 2024.
Economists polled by Reuters had expected the bank to keep rates steady at 5.75%.
The Bank of Indonesia said the move was to strengthen the currency and a preemptive measure to keep inflation in its target range of 1.5% to 3.5%.
The Indonesian rupiah depreciated to a record low of 18,285 against the greenback on Tuesday, while the inflation rate in the country was at 3.23% in October.
Markets in Asia ended mostly higher on Wednesday in choppy trading as investors assessed Nvidia earnings, Japan exports data, and comments from global leaders at the APEC summit in China.
South Korea's Kospi led gains in the region as chip heavyweights rose, rising 2% to 5,067.44. The small-cap Kosdaq also advanced 2% to close at 662.81.
Japan's Nikkei 225 gained 0.28% to close at 59,024.28, while the broad-broad Topix lost 0.42% to 3,824.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was 0.87% lower in its final hour of trade, while the CSI 300 on mainland China advanced 0.18% to 3,983
